title: Fifty-Two Lookalikes
description: Why a shuffled deck defeats raw memory, the plan for beating it, and your baseline score

concepts.title: How it works: two features, endless mix-ups
concepts.contentHtml:
Someone shuffles a deck, fans it under your nose and asks you to remember the order. Where do you even start? The trouble is not only the number of cards. Every card is built from the same few parts, 13 values and 4 suits, mixed and matched. The 7 of hearts shares its value with three other cards and its suit with twelve more, so it has fifteen close relatives in the pack.

Psychologists have caught this kind of muddle in the act. In 1992 M. T. Reinitz, W. J. Lammers and B. P. Cochran showed people nonsense words and faces, then tested which ones they recognised. People often claimed to have seen a new item if they had previously seen items containing its parts.1 They made many more false alarms for conjunction items, built by combining features of two separate studied items, than for items that mixed one studied feature with a new one, and in recall, conjunction errors were much more common than errors with new features.2 The authors concluded that features of stored items keep some independence in memory and can be wrongly recombined.3

Cards were not part of that experiment, but a deck is a trap of exactly this shape. Study the 7 of hearts and the 9 of spades, and an hour later the 7 of spades can feel familiar, though it was never there. The cure is to stop storing two loose features. A 2023 paper co-written by the memory athlete Nelson Dellis puts the aim of every card system in one line: to turn each card in a 52 card deck into something memorable.4 In this skill that something is a single, whole face. The 7 of hearts becomes a rock star, and a rock star has no suit to swap.

concepts.title: Drill: your baseline deck
concepts.contentHtml:
Before you learn a single face, measure what you can do without one. This is the same honest start as the baseline word list in How Memory Works, but with cards, and this time you will also count one special kind of mistake.

  1. Read the ten cards below once, about five seconds each, saying each one aloud.
  2. Use no tricks. No pictures and no stories yet. Just look and say.
  3. Clear your head for a minute: count backwards from 50 in sevens.
  4. Write the ten cards down in order without looking.
  5. Score two numbers: cards in the right place, and swaps, where you had the right value with the wrong suit or the right suit with the wrong value. A swap is a conjunction error caught in the act.
Drill Your baseline: read these ten cards once, then follow steps 3 to 5. The quiz will ask for them.
  1. 7 of hearts
  2. 9 of spades
  3. queen of diamonds
  4. 7 of clubs
  5. 2 of hearts
  6. king of spades
  7. 9 of diamonds
  8. ace of clubs
  9. 4 of hearts
  10. jack of spades

The list is mean on purpose. Two sevens, two nines and a run of spades: it is built from repeated parts, just like a real deck, so swaps get every chance to appear. Keep both scores somewhere safe. In Lesson 5 you will memorise a fresh set of cards with the whole system and put the two results side by side.

concepts.title: Myth check: the card sharp's memory
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Memory champions photograph the deck in their heads.
Reality Ask one. When Ben Pridmore of Nottingham won the World Memory Championships in 2009, his second title in a row, NPR asked how he did it. Decks of cards, he said, were the easiest thing for him, and he described the method like this: "What we do basically is we transform the information in front of us, numbers, into images of people, of objects, and we visualize these people and objects interacting, forming a story along a mental journey.1" No photographs: images and a route, which is exactly what this skill builds.
Myth If you can memorise a deck, you can beat a casino.
Reality When the host joked that Pridmore had better be kept out of casinos, he replied that it actually doesn't quite work like that.2 Card counting, which this course does not teach, is a rough running tally of high and low cards already seen, not a record of their order.

Wait, really? The number of possible orders of a deck is 52 × 51 × 50 and so on all the way down to 1, a number 68 digits long, about 8 followed by 67 zeros. You will never hold the possibilities in your head, and you do not need to. You need 52 faces and a route, and then any order at all becomes a walk past people you know.

tryIt: Deal ten cards from a shuffled deck, study them for one minute, write down the order, and count how many mistakes had the right value but the wrong suit.

title: Every Card a Number
description: One rule turns the forty number cards into pegs you already own: suit by sound, value by digit

concepts.title: How it works: decode the suit
concepts.contentHtml:
You already own a hundred images. In Numbers into Words you built a peg for every pair of digits from 00 to 99, with tyre for 14 and cat for 71. A deck needs only 52 images, so the cheapest card system is a rule that turns each card into a two-digit number and borrows its peg. Here is the rule this course uses, made from the major system's own sound code.

The suit gives the first digit. Say the suit's name and decode its first consonant sound: spade starts with s, so 0; diamond starts with d, so 1; club starts with a hard c, so 7. Heart is the clever one. The h is free in the major system, so the first sound that counts is the r, and hearts are 4. The value gives the second digit: an ace is 1, two to nine are themselves, and the ten is 0.

So the 7 of hearts is 47, which is rock, and the 4 of diamonds is 14, your old friend the tyre. Spades fill 00 to 09, diamonds 10 to 19, hearts 40 to 49 and clubs 70 to 79. Because every peg in a suit starts with that suit's sound, you can often tell the suit before you finish decoding: soot, sumo and seal are spades; rat, ram and rope are hearts.

Twelve court cards are left over, because a suit has 13 cards and there are only ten digits. Lesson 3 gives every king, queen and jack a face of its own. The idea underneath, a code that turns each card into something you already know, runs through every card system you will meet; this one simply recycles work you have already done.

concepts.title: Drill: forty pegs
concepts.contentHtml:
Most of these pegs are already in your 00 to 99 list. Where your own list has a different word for a number, keep yours and change the card: one word per number, for good.

  1. Learn one suit at a time, starting with whichever decade of your peg list you know best.
  2. Say every step aloud. 7 of hearts: heart is 4, seven is 7, 47, rock. It is slow at first, and that is fine.
  3. Mind the sounds. The b in tomb and comb is silent, so they are 13 and 73. The s in toes and rose sounds like z, which is still 0. W, h and y are free like the vowels, so sewer is 04 and rower 44. Count every written r, even where your accent drops it, just as tyre is 14 in your peg list.
  4. Deal and decode. Shuffle the forty number cards, turn them one at a time and say the peg.
  5. Place ten. Put the ten cards below on the first ten loci of your palace, one peg per locus, and walk the route.
Drill Ten cards and their pegs. Place one per locus and walk the route forwards and back. The quiz will ask for them in order.
  1. 3 of spades: sumo
  2. 7 of hearts: rock
  3. ace of clubs: cat
  4. 4 of diamonds: tyre
  5. 10 of hearts: rose
  6. 9 of clubs: cop
  7. 2 of diamonds: tin
  8. 8 of spades: sofa
  9. 5 of hearts: rail
  10. 6 of clubs: cage

Notice how the suit sound helps when you walk back: if the image at locus 8 is a sofa, its s tells you it is a spade before you have even reached the f.

concepts.title: Myth check: one right system
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth There is one proper card system, and the champions all use it.
Reality A 2023 paper on memory athletics notes that there are several systems for memorising cards.1 The best known is the Dominic System of the former memory champion Dominic O'Brien, which uses letters instead of sounds. The value becomes a letter (1 is A, 2 is B, 3 is C) and the suit adds its own initial, so the 5 of clubs is E, C.2 Then you choose a person with those initials: Nelson Dellis, a co-author of the paper, chose Eric Clapton.
Myth A system only works if you follow its rules to the letter.
Reality Dellis could not find a good person for the 4 of spades, D, S. It reminded him of the Nintendo DS, which reminded him of Super Mario, so his 4 of spades is Mario.3 The paper says plainly that it is often better to choose something intuitive, so that the mapping is easier to remember4 and less time is spent working out who a card is. The same goes for your pegs: if sewer leaves you cold for the 4 of spades, choose another word for 04 and change your peg list to match.

Wait, really? Some champions go far bigger. Ben Pridmore told NPR in 2009 that he has a picture for each three-digit number: 994 is his brother-in-law, 570 is Lisa Simpson and 892 is a telephone.5 That is a thousand images, against your hundred. Lesson 4 looks at what extra images buy and what they cost.

tryIt: Deal the forty number cards one at a time, say each card's number and peg aloud, and time the whole pass so you can beat it tomorrow.

title: A Face for Every Card
description: Turning pegs into people, faces for the twelve court cards, and why people stick

concepts.title: How it works: why faces?
concepts.contentHtml:
A peg can sit on a locus, but it cannot do much there. A tyre just lies around; a cyclist pumping up a tyre is a scene. That is why most card systems end in people. Pridmore describes his images as people and objects, and the Dominic System picks a person for every card from the start.

There is good evidence that people make strong anchors. In 1977 T. B. Rogers, N. A. Kuiper and W. S. Kirker asked volunteers to rate adjectives in different ways: by how they looked, how they sounded, what they meant, or whether they described the volunteer. Adjectives rated under the self-reference task were recalled best,1 and the authors called self-reference a rich and powerful encoding process.2 Twenty years later C. S. Symons and B. T. Johnson pooled the research in a meta-analysis. The effect held up, but it was smaller when the comparison was relating words to another person rather than judging their meaning,3 so linking things to other people captures part of the same benefit. Their explanation is that the self is a well-developed and often-used construct that promotes elaboration and organisation.4

So your card images should be people and creatures you can see clearly and who come with habits of their own. The rule for the forty number cards is short. If the peg is already a person or an animal, it is the face: sumo, cop, cat, rat. If the peg is a thing, the face is whoever uses it: the tyre's face is a cyclist, the sewer's is a plumber and the tomb's is a mummy. Your 00 to 99 list stays exactly as it is; each card simply gains a body.

concepts.title: Drill: the court and the crowd
concepts.contentHtml:
The court cards get faces by theme rather than by number. Give each suit a world and each rank a role in it. Hearts are love, diamonds are riches, clubs are anything with a club, and spades dig, for treasure, in gardens and in the dark. The king is the most powerful figure in that world, the queen its leading lady and the jack its young rogue or worker.

  1. Learn the court by suit. Say the theme, then the three faces: diamonds are riches, so Midas, the diva and the jewel thief.
  2. Meet the crowd. Go through the forty number-card faces ten a day, picturing each face holding its peg: the cyclist with a tyre, the plumber up to his knees in a sewer.
  3. Swap the duds. If a face will not come alive, use someone you know who fits. Nelson Dellis made his own father the king of hearts, because hearts made him think of family.1
  4. Test both ways. Card to face, then face to card: plumber, so sewer, so 04, so the 4 of spades.
Drill The twelve court faces. Learn them by suit, cover the list and recite all twelve. The quiz will ask for them.
  1. king of hearts: Henry VIII
  2. queen of hearts: a bride
  3. jack of hearts: Romeo
  4. king of diamonds: King Midas
  5. queen of diamonds: an opera diva
  6. jack of diamonds: a jewel thief
  7. king of clubs: a caveman
  8. queen of clubs: a golfer
  9. jack of clubs: a juggler
  10. king of spades: a pirate
  11. queen of spades: a witch
  12. jack of spades: a gardener

concepts.title: Myth check: who is on the cards?
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth The kings and queens in a pack are portraits of real monarchs, and the queen is Elizabeth I.
Reality According to the International Playing-Card Society, the courts of the standard English pattern are not thought to represent anyone and have never carried names.1 Elizabeth I cannot be the queen either: she was born in 1533, after the courts were designed.2

Yet giving every card a face is an old idea. French cardmakers around 1470 invented the suit signs you know, which the French call spearheads, hearts, trefoils and squares,3 so the spade was never a garden tool and the digging theme in this course is a pun. At the beginning, French court cards were labelled as particular heroes and heroines from Scripture, history and fable, and French cards of the Paris pattern still carry names:4 the king of hearts is Charles, the king of spades David, the king of diamonds Caesar and the king of clubs Alexander.

Wait, really? The king of hearts looks as if he is stabbing himself in the head, which is why players call him the Suicide King. On early English cards he swung an axe. Poor copying by the blockmakers lost the axe head over the years, and the shaft turned into a sword that seems to be driven into his head. A card face that drifted for centuries is a good warning for your own list: when you change a face, change it on purpose, and change it everywhere.

tryIt: Go through the twelve court cards and replace any face that will not come alive with someone you know who fits the suit's theme.

title: Person, Action, Object
description: Three cards in one scene with PAO, the full list of actions and objects, and how many loci a deck needs

concepts.title: How it works: three cards, one scene
concepts.contentHtml:
One face per locus works, but then a whole deck needs 52 loci. Memory athletes squeeze harder with person-action-object, or PAO. The 2023 paper co-written by Nelson Dellis describes it: every card gets a distinctive person, and each person is given an action and an object that relate to them.1 Dellis's 5 of clubs is Eric Clapton, playing an instrument, with a guitar.2

When a deck arrives, you take the cards three at a time: the person of the first, the action of the second and the object of the third, fused into one scene on one locus. In one of Dellis's examples, three cards became C-3PO playing a pizza as a guitar.3 To read it back you walk the route and run the code in reverse: the person gives card one, the action card two, the object card three. As the paper puts it, the problem of recalling 52 cards is reduced to recalling 17 unique scenes.4

Count it yourself: 17 scenes hold 51 cards, so one card is left over. In the paper's account it is remembered without the palace, worked out by elimination as the only card not yet seen, or stored in an 18th position.5 That gives three classic palace sizes for one deck:

  • 52 loci, one face per place: the simplest start.
  • 26 loci, two faces meeting at each place.
  • 18 loci with PAO: 17 full scenes and one last card.

The paper adds that PAO is the technique of Shijir-Erdene Bat-Enkh,6 who held the Speed Cards world record when it was written.

concepts.title: Drill: your first scenes
concepts.contentHtml:
Here is the full PAO list for this course. Every card keeps the face from Lesson 3 and gains an action and an object that belong to that face, so the cyclist inflates, the plumber plunges and the pirate buries. No action or object is used twice, so every scene decodes only one way.

  1. Learn each action and object with its face. Picture the face doing its own action with its own object: Zeus zapping with his thunderbolt.
  2. Take three cards and say person, action, object aloud: rock star (7 of hearts), tripping over (2 of clubs), binoculars (9 of spades).
  3. Make one moving scene on a locus: a rock star in leather trousers trips over a pair of binoculars on your doormat.
  4. Decode as you check. Rock star, so rock, so 47, the 7 of hearts. Tripping over is Charlie Chaplin's action, so cane, 72, the 2 of clubs.
  5. Next three, next locus, and never let one scene leak into the next.
Drill Nine cards make three scenes on your first three loci; the first scene is the worked example above. The quiz will ask for the cards.
  1. 7 of hearts
  2. 2 of clubs
  3. 9 of spades
  4. king of diamonds
  5. 3 of diamonds
  6. 5 of spades
  7. ace of hearts
  8. 10 of clubs
  9. jack of spades

concepts.title: Myth check: bigger is better
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Three cards in one picture will blur together.
Reality Dellis reports the opposite. While memorising, he looks at the three cards one by one but perceives a single composite image,1 and he compares it to reading a sentence: when he encodes a triple at one place, he does not think about the previous three cards or the next three at all.
Myth The more cards each image holds, the better.
Reality Every gain is paid for in learning. One face per card means 52 images and 52 loci. PAO means 156 things to learn, 52 people, 52 actions and 52 objects, but only 18 loci. Pridmore's thousand number images show how far the trade can go. Start with faces alone, and add the actions and objects once the faces come instantly.

Wait, really? Similar faces are the enemy, and athletes design against them. Dellis has two basketball players in his list, Kobe Bryant and Shaquille O'Neal. Both could be shooting a basketball, so he gave Bryant dribbling and O'Neal dunking instead,2 and he reports that this cut the time it took to learn his PAO list. The paper states the rule outright: no action or object may be assigned to two different cards.3 That is why your tables give the hairdresser combing and the cat scratching, and never both of them grooming.

tryIt: Deal six cards, turn them into two PAO scenes on the first two loci of your palace, and read the cards back an hour later.

title: Drilling the Deck
description: From decoding to knowing at a glance: flashcard drills, the race for speed, and a rematch with your baseline

concepts.title: How it works: from code to glance
concepts.contentHtml:
Right now the 7 of hearts is a little sum: heart is 4, seven is 7, 47, rock, rock star. It works, but it is slow, and a deck is 52 sums. The point of drilling is to skip the sum, until the card simply looks like a rock star.

Psychologists call this automatisation. In 1991 B. J. Compton and Gordon Logan compared two memory-based theories of it, which both describe automatisation as a transition from algorithmic processing, working the answer out, to memory retrieval, simply knowing it.1 Their volunteers checked equations in alphabet arithmetic, such as H + 3 = K,2 which you first solve by counting along the alphabet, and reported their strategy on each trial. The mixture model predicted that using both routes on one trial would be slower than the algorithm alone; the race model predicted the reverse. The results supported the race model: the two routes run side by side, and practice gives memory the chance to finish first.

Your card code is the algorithm, and your faces are the memories waiting to win the race. Memory athletes describe the same journey. The 2023 paper on Dellis's method says that mapping a card to its associations eventually becomes automatic: athletes look at a card and automatically think of the person associated with it.3 For Speed Cards, it adds, this is critical, because the speed of memorisation often comes down to how quickly the cards can be encoded.4

concepts.title: Drill: the rematch
concepts.contentHtml:
Drill your faces like flashcards, little and often, then test the whole system against your Lesson 1 baseline.

  1. Flash, do not study. Shuffle, turn each card and say its face aloud. Aim to see the face, not to compute it.
  2. Time the pass through all 52 cards and write the time down.
  3. Catch the slow ones. Any card that makes you work out the sum goes in a pile to practise first next time. If a face keeps failing, change it.
  4. Space it. Short daily passes beat one long session, as How Memory Works showed.
  5. Rematch. When the faces come quickly, memorise the twelve cards below: one face per locus on twelve loci, or PAO on four.
  6. Score it as in Lesson 1: cards in the right place, and swaps. Put the numbers beside your baseline.
Drill The rematch: twelve cards, with the whole system this time. The quiz will ask for them in order.
  1. 6 of clubs
  2. queen of hearts
  3. 3 of spades
  4. 8 of diamonds
  5. 10 of hearts
  6. 4 of clubs
  7. jack of diamonds
  8. 5 of hearts
  9. 2 of spades
  10. king of clubs
  11. 9 of hearts
  12. ace of diamonds

Look hard at the swaps column. In Lesson 1 the 7 of hearts could leak into the 7 of clubs; now one is a rock star and the other a geek, and a rock star cannot turn into a geek halfway through a walk. When The Whole Deck asks for 13, then 26, then all 52 cards, these are the faces you will use.

concepts.title: Myth check: shuffles and sharp pictures
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Two or three shuffles make a practice deck random.
Reality In 1992 Dave Bayer and Persi Diaconis showed that after seven random riffle shuffles of a deck of 52 cards, every order is nearly equally likely;1 shuffle less, and the deck is far from random. The gentle overhand shuffle is much worse: it takes about 2,500 of them.2 After only two or three shuffles there are still visible patterns from the old order,3 and a lazily shuffled practice deck can hand you runs you have already learned.
Myth Faster memorising needs ever sharper, more detailed pictures.
Reality Dellis reports the reverse. As a novice he spent time making his images vivid, picturing his father's hair, accent and height. Under the time pressure of competition the detail dropped away by itself,4 and now he mainly imagines the essence of his father's hair. His ace of spades is Arnold Schwarzenegger, yet he does not see Schwarzenegger at all: he only hears his voice,5 and in a PAO scene the action is done by a "blob".

Wait, really? Dellis says the fading happened automatically, not on purpose,6 and that using a sound as the main image for a person is rare in his list.7 The lesson for your drills is modest: a face that fires instantly can carry its card on a hint, so practise for speed of recognition rather than prettier pictures, and do not worry when the detail fades.

tryIt: Riffle shuffle a deck seven times, flip through it saying each face aloud against a timer, and set aside the five slowest cards to practise tomorrow.
